title: Validate the whole input
summary: Why IsMatch without anchors is a validation bug, \A...\z for full-string checks, and word boundaries \b and \B (Unicode-aware in .NET).

steps.title: IsMatch finds a part, validation needs the whole
body: `Regex.IsMatch` answers "is there a match **somewhere**?". That is right for search and wrong for validation:
Regex.IsMatch("bob; DROP TABLE users", @"[a-z0-9_]{3,16}")     // true: "bob" is in there
For validation, pin the pattern to both ends with `\A ... \z`. .NET has no `FullMatch` method (Python has
`re.fullmatch`), so the anchors are your job.
Validation is defence in depth, not your SQL injection fix: queries still use parameters. But a validator that
checks only part of the input lets through exactly the strings an attacker would send. Below, the unanchored

steps.prompt: A user name is 3 to 16 lowercase letters, digits or underscores. Which check is correct?
steps.explain: Without anchors any 3-letter run passes. With only `\A`, `bob; DROP` passes. With `$`, `bob\n` passes. Only `\A ... \z` checks the whole string and nothing more.

steps.title: Symptom: the sign-up validator lets anything in
prompt: **Symptom.** The security team found accounts named `bob; DROP TABLE users` and `eve` followed by a newline.
The sign-up service checks names with `Regex.IsMatch(name, pattern)`, and these checks run the same way: a name
is accepted when the pattern finds a match anywhere in it.
The rule: 3 to 16 lowercase letters, digits or underscores, and nothing else. Fix the pattern.
hints: The pattern must start at the start of the input and end at its very end.
`$` still accepts the trailing newline. Use `\A` at the start and `\z` at the end.
steps.explain: `\A[a-z0-9_]{3,16}\z` leaves no room before or after. `^...$` fixes the first account but not the second: `$` matches before the final newline, which then lands in your database and your logs.

steps.title: Word boundaries: \b and \B
body: `\b` is a position between a **word character** (`\w`) and a non-word character, or the start or end of the text.
`\B` is any position that is not a boundary.
- `\bcat\b` finds `cat` alone, not in `concat` or `cats`. This is what `rg -w` and `grep -w` do.
- `\Bcat` finds `cat` only inside a longer word, like `concat`.
1. `_` is a word character, so `\bid\b` does **not** find the `id` in `user_id`. A dash is not, so it finds it in
2. In .NET, `\w` is Unicode, so `\b` is too: `\bcafé\b` works. In JavaScript `\b` is ASCII only, even with the `u`
flag, so the same pattern fails after the `é`.

steps.explain: `\bcat\b` finds the first `cat` and the one before the dot. `\Bcat` finds only the `cat` inside `concat`. In .NET `é` is a word character, so there is a boundary between it and the space.

steps.title: The IP, and not its neighbours
prompt: Back to the firewall logs from module 1: `10\.0\.0\.1` also finds `10.0.0.12` and `110.0.0.1`. Find the address
hints: Digits are word characters, so a boundary sits between `1` and `:` but not between `1` and `2`.
steps.explain: The boundaries refuse a digit on either side. One edge remains: `10.0.0.1.5` still matches, because a dot is not a word character. For strict IP handling, parse with `System.Net.IPAddress`.

steps.prompt: Does `\bid\b` find a match in each text?
steps.explain: Spaces, `=`, brackets and dashes are not word characters, so they make boundaries. Letters and `_` are, so `userid`, `ids` and `user_id` have no boundary next to the `id`.

steps.title: The word error
prompt: An alert should fire on lines that contain the word `error`, in lower case, as a word of its own. Metric names like
`errors=0` and `error_code=5`, and words like `terror`, must not fire it.
hints: Put a boundary on both sides of the word.
`\berror\b`. Remember that `_` counts as a word character.
steps.explain: `error_code` has no boundary after `error`, because `_` is a word character. That is usually what you want for identifiers, and a surprise when you expected `_` to separate words.

steps.title: A user name validator that holds
prompt: Write `bool IsValidUsername(string name)`. A valid name:
- uses only lowercase ASCII letters, ASCII digits and `_`,
Return true only when the **whole** name follows the rules: no trailing newline, nothing after it. Use
template: Dojo.Eq("16 characters is valid", true, IsValidUsername("a_very_long_name"));
Dojo.Eq("17 characters is too long", false, IsValidUsername("a_very_long_name_"));
Dojo.Eq("2 characters is too short", false, IsValidUsername("ab"));
Dojo.Eq("a trailing newline is rejected", false, IsValidUsername("bob\n"));
Dojo.Eq("bob; DROP TABLE users is rejected", false, IsValidUsername("bob; DROP TABLE users"));
Dojo.Eq("starting with a digit is rejected", false, IsValidUsername("9lives"));
Dojo.Eq("starting with _ is rejected", false, IsValidUsername("_bob"));
Dojo.Eq("non-ASCII letters are rejected", false, IsValidUsername("bøb"));
Dojo.Eq("the empty string is rejected", false, IsValidUsername(""));
hints: One letter first, then 2 to 15 more allowed characters: 3 to 16 in total.
